problem: Imitation-learned sidewalk navigation policies suffer from compounding errors, goal-driven shortcut behavior, weak social compliance, and a generalization-precision dilemma: pretraining on diverse fleet data does not give precise control for a specific robot instance. Common action heads (Gaussian, diffusion, anchor regression) are either unimodal, too noisy, or oversmoothed.
motivation: Food-delivery robots and wheelchairs must travel long distances on sidewalks with only a monocular RGB camera and noisy GPS, under strict compute limits. Large-scale pretraining gives a generalist prior, but deployment-specific safety and social norms need corrective human feedback, which is sparse and comparative rather than dense demonstrations.
key_idea: Pretrain an anchored flow-matching policy (K-means anchors plus flow refinement, with gated cross-attention to curb goal shortcuts) on large fleet data, then align it to a specific robot with reward-free, DPO-style preference learning on human-intervention pairs (corrective action preferred over policy action).
insight: Gated cross-attention reduces attention sink on the goal token. In the closed-loop ablation, removing it (w/o GCA) drops SR from 0.42 to 0.29 and RC from 0.66 to 0.59. Reference-policy regularization matters for alignment: w/o Ref. gets SR 0.29 versus 0.55 on R0. Not pushing down the rejected continuous action, and instead anchoring it to its prior, keeps finetuning stable. Small amounts of intervention data (46-91K) give large gains, including on shifted robot dynamics and cameras (R1, R2).
method: Anchored flow matching: K=64 anchor trajectories from constrained K-means over normalized actions; each expert trajectory is assigned to its nearest anchor; rectified-flow velocity regression on anchor-noised trajectories with a Beta(1.5,1) timestep; a scoring head predicts the anchor via CE; 4 inference steps.

Gated cross-attention: sigmoid gating on keys and values of the context (scene tokens plus goal token) to mitigate attention sink on the goal; goal token dropped with p=0.9 during training to avoid shortcuts.

Encoder and auxiliary losses: FastViT-MA36 on 11 frames at 352x128 (past-frame tokens via global average pooling, current-frame patch tokens); self-attention; auxiliary visual-odometry and trajectory heads; embodiment-ID token and dataset-specific normalization for mixed-data pretraining.

Three-stage training: pretraining on a mixture of public and fleet datasets, SFT on the 300 h sidewalk fleet dataset (48.5K segments, 281 robots), then LoRA preference alignment (rank 16 on attention projections).

Preference alignment loss: a DPO-style score-level margin between the preferred anchor h+ and rejected anchor h-, plus a KL regularizer to the reference scoring head. Velocity loss: regress toward the corrective trajectory x+, and pull the rejected mode toward its anchor prior. A stop-gradient reference velocity regularizer and the original FM loss are also included.

Intervention data collection: a human takes over via joystick in the real world (about 13K frames); in simulation an ORCA/A* expert takes over when ADE > 1 m or on unsafe states. The pair (policy trajectory, corrected trajectory) forms the preference sample.
Deployment: waypoint output tracked by a simple PD controller (vmax 1.5 m/s), so the policy is platform-agnostic (wheeled robot, Go2, G1).

setting.backbone: FastViT-MA36 encoder + transformer anchored flow-matching policy (trained; LoRA preference finetuning)
setting.training_data: Pretraining on a mixture of public robot and driving datasets (GNM-family, SACSoN, EgoWalk, GND, NavSim, etc.); SFT on the ~300 h / 19.4M-frame fleet teleoperation dataset (281 robots); preference finetuning on ~13K real frames of intervention data plus simulated interventions (46K-91K)
setting.observation: monocular RGB history (11 frames at 20 Hz, 352x128) + noisy GPS goal + pose
setting.action_space: predicted 4-second waypoint trajectory (20 steps at 5 Hz; Δx, Δy, Δθ) tracked by a PD controller
setting.privileged: none at test time (the A*/ORCA expert is used only for simulated intervention data in training)

results: FlowPilot-IL reaches SR 0.42 / RC 0.66 in closed-loop simulation, beating the strongest baseline S2E (0.35 / 0.55). Preference finetuning raises R0 SR to 0.55 and improves the novel robots R1 and R2. In the real world, preference finetuning cuts IR by 40.0% and NIR by 52.1% relative to the base model, and both variants far outperform ViNT, NoMaD, and CityWalker.
limitations: Monocular RGB has scale ambiguity and struggles with textureless or reflective obstacles.
Overly conservative behavior and deadlocks in crowded, narrow, or crosswalk scenes, requiring human intervention.
Human interventions were needed for alignment, and real-world baselines were not repeatedly deployed in the expanded 17.8 km evaluation for safety reasons.
